AC runs but rooms stay warm Book soon

Likely causes

  • Restricted airflow can reduce cooling even while the indoor fan runs.
  • A refrigerant leak can leave the system unable to remove enough heat.
  • An outdoor unit fault can interrupt cooling while air still moves indoors.

Check safely first

  • Confirm cooling mode and compare the set temperature with the displayed room temperature.
  • With cooling off, inspect an accessible filter according to the equipment instructions; leave enclosed parts closed.
  • Note whether all rooms are warm or only one area; report the pattern when booking.

What the technician does

A technician checks whether cooling is being produced and whether it reaches the rooms. Share the room pattern to help locate the fault.

The diagnosis determines the repair scope; parts and access can require a return visit.

When to act: Book a diagnostic; stop cooling if ice or repeated trips appear; for a burning smell, leave and call 911 from outside.

Likely causes

  • An electrical fault can prevent the outdoor unit from starting.
  • A refrigerant problem can reduce heat removal despite apparent operation.

Check safely first

  • Check the thermostat display for cooling mode and any visible message.
  • Observe the outdoor unit from ground level; do not remove panels or reach through the grille.

A technician checks the cooling request and outdoor operation. Mention any storm or outage immediately before cooling stopped.

Scheduling depends on availability; same-day service is available when the schedule allows.

AC starts and stops repeatedly Book soon

Likely causes

  • A thermostat or control signal can interrupt the cooling request.
  • Restricted airflow can contribute to unstable operation.
  • An electrical or refrigerant fault can cause protective shutdowns.

Check safely first

  • Note the start and stop pattern without repeatedly changing the temperature setting.
  • Check the thermostat for an error message from its normal user screen.
  • Observe whether a nearby supply vent blows directly toward the thermostat.
  • Leave equipment panels closed and avoid repeated manual restarts.

What the technician does

A technician observes when operation stops and tests the interruption. Record cycle timing before the visit without forcing additional restarts.

Intermittent faults may need observation before the repair can be confirmed.

When to act: Stop cooling if rapid restarts continue, especially with unusual sounds.

Ice forms on the coil or refrigerant line Book soon

Likely causes

  • Restricted indoor airflow can allow an evaporator coil to freeze.
  • A refrigerant leak can create operating conditions that lead to icing.
  • An indoor fan fault can limit airflow across the coil.

Check safely first

  • Turn cooling off at the thermostat and allow ice to melt naturally.
  • Inspect only an accessible filter with equipment off; follow the equipment instructions.
  • Keep clear of meltwater near electrical equipment; do not open the coil enclosure.

What the technician does

Thawing comes before operating tests. A technician then traces the cause of freezing and checks the meltwater path.

Thawing and access can extend the visit or delay operating tests.

When to act: Turn cooling off and arrange service; do not chip or heat the ice.

Likely causes

  • A blocked condensate path can send cooling water outside its intended drain.
  • A failed pump can leave collected water unable to drain.
  • Ice melting from a frozen coil can overwhelm the normal water path.

Check safely first

  • Turn cooling off and note where the water first appears from a safe distance.
  • Protect nearby belongings only if the area is dry and safe to enter.
  • Do not handle wet wiring or attempt to open a pump or drain enclosure.

What the technician does

A technician locates the water source and checks drainage. Report any ceiling damage or water near wiring when booking.

Active water damage needs prompt attention; repair timing depends on the failed component.

When to act: Stop cooling if water is pooling, reaching wiring or damaging the building.

Likely causes

  • Damaged wiring can create a fault that interrupts power.
  • A motor or starting component can draw abnormal current.
  • A circuit or equipment problem can trigger the breaker during cooling.

Check safely first

  • Stop requesting cooling at the thermostat.
  • Note which breaker tripped without opening the electrical panel cover.
  • For a burning smell or visible smoke, leave the building and call 911 from outside. Report water near the equipment.
  • Stay away from hot, wet or damaged electrical equipment and arrange qualified help.

A technician distinguishes an equipment fault from a circuit problem. Leave the circuit off until qualified help establishes a safe restart.

Testing and any separate electrical work determine the restoration time.

Pricing

What determines the AC repair price?

The repair price follows the diagnosed fault rather than the symptom alone. City & Suburban provides upfront pricing with no hidden fees. Ask about the service-call charge, included checks and any credit toward the repair when booking.

1 The diagnosed faultWarm air can come from several different failures. A control repair, an airflow correction and refrigerant leak work have different scopes. The estimate should identify the cause and explain why the proposed work addresses it.
2 Required partsThe exact part depends on the equipment model and confirmed failure. Availability can affect both the repair path and a return visit. Compare the specified component and labor rather than assuming every starting problem needs the same replacement.
3 Refrigerant and leak workRefrigerant type, leak location and the amount of work required to restore operation affect the decision. Ask whether the scope addresses the leak itself. Recurring refill requests deserve a repair-or-replace discussion based on the actual findings.
4 Indoor and rooftop accessA readily accessible unit presents different work conditions from equipment reached through shared spaces or rooftop entry. Building rules and HOA requirements should be disclosed when booking. Access constraints can affect the visit and any follow-up work.
5 Secondary damageA failed component may be only part of the repair when water has overflowed or the equipment has operated under abnormal conditions. The findings should distinguish the original fault from additional damage. That separation helps explain the complete proposed scope.
6 Testing and follow-upAn intermittent shutdown may require observation that a visible failed part does not. An iced system must thaw before some operating tests are meaningful. The quote should explain any follow-up work and how the repair result will be checked.

Find the fault across the connected system

Central air conditioner

A central air conditioner can lose cooling while indoor air still moves. The symptom should be traced through the connected system before a failed component is assumed. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models.

Evaporator coil

Ice or water around the indoor cooling equipment can point toward an airflow, refrigerant or drainage problem. The evaporator coil needs evaluation in context; visible ice alone does not establish that the coil must be replaced.

Air handler

The air handler moves indoor air through the cooling system. Reduced airflow can affect rooms throughout the home and contribute to icing. A cooling diagnostic should distinguish an airflow fault from an outdoor equipment problem.

Thermostat and controls

A normal thermostat display does not prove that the cooling request reaches the equipment. Controls and wiring belong in the diagnostic when operation is intermittent or the outdoor unit stays silent. Record user-facing messages before the visit.

Outdoor unit

Starting problems, unusual noise and breaker trips require different checks from an indoor water leak. Observe only from a safe location and leave panels closed. Rooftop equipment needs safe building access arranged before the appointment.

Furnace-connected cooling

A furnace can share indoor airflow with a central cooling system. Air moving through that cabinet does not prove that the outdoor cooling equipment is operating. Heating faults belong on the heating repair page.

AC repair questions

Can City & Suburban repair AC the same day?

City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows. Scheduling and repair completion are separate: rooftop access, thawing an iced system or obtaining a part can extend the work. Report the symptom and any building access requirements when requesting an appointment.

What can be checked safely before an AC repair visit?

Safe checks stay at the normal user controls: confirm cooling mode, read the thermostat display and inspect an accessible filter with equipment off. Keep panels closed. Ice, water near wiring or repeated breaker trips are reasons to stop cooling and arrange service. For a burning smell or smoke, leave the building and call 911 from outside.

Is there a charge for an AC diagnostic?

City & Suburban provides upfront pricing with no hidden fees and diagnoses the fault before any repair is quoted. When booking, ask about the service-call charge, what the diagnostic visit includes and whether any of it is credited toward a completed repair. The repair price then comes in writing for approval before work starts.

Should a frozen AC keep running until the technician arrives?

Cooling should be turned off when visible ice appears. Allow the ice to melt naturally; scraping or applying heat can damage the equipment. A diagnostic should then check the airflow and refrigerant conditions that caused freezing. Water from thawing also needs attention if it threatens the building.

Is a leaking AC always a refrigerant leak?

Water around indoor equipment may come from the condensate path, a pump problem or melting ice. Liquid appearance alone cannot identify the source. Dan F., Apr 2026, reported a leak that Rob and Eddie traced to a bad pump. Stop cooling for active overflow or water near electrical equipment.

Can an older AC still be repaired?

Age alone does not settle the decision. The failed part, overall condition, repair history and refrigerant requirements matter together. City & Suburban provides upfront pricing with no hidden fees. Compare the proposed repair with the condition of the remaining equipment before choosing the next step.

What should happen when an AC uses an older refrigerant?

Identify the refrigerant from the equipment information before comparing repair options. The leak location, required work and availability of the correct material affect the decision. A repair quote should explain those limits. Avoid assumptions that every old unit must be replaced or only needs a refill.

Can City & Suburban service rooftop AC at a condo?

City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, including rooftop and condo-mounted cooling equipment. Building access and HOA requirements should be shared when booking. Isaac F., Aug 2025, described an AC fault traced to damaged wiring on the roof of the building.

How long does an AC repair take?

Repair timing follows diagnosis. An accessible component fault may be simpler than an intermittent shutdown, a refrigerant leak or a system that must thaw first. Parts availability and roof access also matter. City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows, without guaranteeing completion that day.

By the City & Suburban team · Updated October 2026 · 18 min read

Air conditioning in Chicago fails on the hottest week of the year, usually in a building that was never designed around it. Cook County Assessor records for single-family and small multi-family homes in the city's eight townships put the median year built at 1927. The condenser ends up on a roof, a back porch or a gangway, and the air handler gets squeezed into a closet. This guide explains what the common symptoms actually mean: warm air at the registers, short cycling, a frozen coil, water where it does not belong, noise outdoors and a breaker that will not hold. It also covers what a thorough repair call measures, and when an old system stops being worth repairing.

Key takeaways

  • Warm air at the registers has two different families of cause: the system is not making cold air, or it is not moving it. The temperature split between return and supply air separates them.
  • Short cycling can come from controls, a safety trip or oversized capacity, and only measured checks separate them. Adding refrigerant without those checks can hide the real fault.
  • Ice on the coil or the copper line means cooling should be turned off. Fan-only thawing suits only dry, safe equipment where the manual allows it; running a compressor through ice can turn a repair into a replacement.
  • Water under an air handler is a condensate problem: a blocked drain line, a failed pump, a float switch or a rusted pan.
  • Repair stops paying when the age of the system multiplied by the quoted repair passes roughly $5,000, or when the system still runs on a refrigerant no longer used in new equipment.

Why is the air conditioner running but blowing warm air?

SHORT ANSWER

Warm air at the vents has two separate causes: the system is not making cold air, or it is not moving it. The temperature split between return and supply air separates the two. Pressures at the outdoor unit then confirm a charge or compressor fault. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, then gives the exact price in writing for approval.

It is mid July, the outdoor temperature sits in the nineties, and the air leaving the registers feels like room air. In a Lakeview three-flat the condenser that runs the air conditioning sits on the roof, out of sight. The air handler hides in a closet two floors below. Nothing looks broken from inside, which is why the call usually comes after a full day of waiting for the house to cool.

The common response is a quick refrigerant top-off. A gauge goes on, and a pound or two goes in. The air gets colder for a few weeks, then the same call comes back in August. The leak that caused the low charge is still there, because nobody looked for it.

Warm air at a register points at one of two mechanisms, and each one calls for a different repair. Either the system is not producing cold air, which points at charge, a leaking coil, a failed compressor or a condenser that never starts. Or it is producing cold air and failing to deliver it. That points at a clogged filter, a weak blower, a failed capacitor or a disconnected duct.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, so the measurements come before any part is named. A normal split moves the search indoors to filter, blower and duct. A small split moves it outside to pressures, superheat and subcooling. A low charge then means finding where the refrigerant went, and the exact price goes in writing before work starts.

That sequence is what customers describe when the fault turns out to be a leak. Nisha J. wrote in June 2026: "Rob investigated the issue carefully and quickly found a refrigerant leak." City & Suburban has worked on Chicago systems since 1952 and holds a 4.98 average across 204 Google reviews.

Why does the air conditioner turn on and off every few minutes?

SHORT ANSWER

Short cycling means the system is being stopped early, either by its controls or by a safety switch. Cycle timing is worth noting, but timing alone does not identify the fault. Pressures read through a full cycle, with control and wiring checks, show whether a pressure switch is tripping or a control is dropping out. Refrigerant added without that data can hide the fault. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted.

In a West Loop condo the system starts, cools for three or four minutes, then stops. It restarts a few minutes later and does the same thing again. The thermostat sits on an interior wall near the kitchen, where cooking heat reaches it first. Rooms furthest from the air handler never catch up, so the setpoint goes lower and the cycling gets faster.

The common response is a new thermostat. Sometimes the setpoint is simply dropped two degrees. Either change can quiet the symptom for a day, and neither touches a safety switch that is doing exactly what it was built to do. Condenser cleaning and filter work belong in a scheduled AC tune-up, not in a second paid visit for the same symptom.

Short cycling comes from three different places. A control fault means the thermostat is reading the wrong air, or a wire is intermittent, so the call for cooling drops out. A protection trip means a pressure switch or an overload shuts the compressor down, usually after a dirty coil or a low charge. Oversized capacity means the system satisfies the thermostat faster than the rooms can mix the air.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted. Short cycles with cold air at the register can come from a control fault, but measured checks have to confirm it. A cycle that ends with the outdoor unit stopping, while the indoor fan runs on, can indicate a protection trip. Coil condition, the filter and the wiring at both ends all belong in the same diagnostic.

Intermittent wiring is a textbook cause, and it rarely shows up on a single meter reading. Isaac F. wrote in August 2025: “Mike and Rob assisted with AC unit issues where the cause was not readily apparent. After diligent troubleshooting, Mike identified the issue as a fraying thermometer wire on the roof of our building and quickly replaced it.” City & Suburban sends NATE-certified technicians.

  • On-cycles of a few minutes with cold air still at the register: thermostat location and wiring are possible causes to check, not a confirmed diagnosis.
  • A cycle that ends with the outdoor unit stopping while the indoor fan runs on: a pressure switch or an overload may be tripping.
  • Cycling that began right after a thermostat swap: the new control may be wired for a different system.
  • Cycling only on hot afternoons: condenser airflow and refrigerant charge are the first suspects.
  • Cycling plus ice on the copper line: treat it as an airflow or charge fault, not a control fault.
  • Safe checks at home: change the air filter, clear leaves and debris from around the outdoor unit, and confirm nothing blocks the return grille.

What causes a frozen AC coil, and what should happen first?

SHORT ANSWER

Ice forms when the evaporator coil runs below freezing, which happens with too little airflow across it or too little refrigerant inside it. The first step is to stop cooling so the coil can thaw, because readings taken on ice mean nothing. Running the fan alone helps only when the equipment is dry and the manual allows it; with overflow or water near wiring, switch the system off and keep away. Airflow and charge then decide which side caused the ice. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted.

A Logan Square basement in August, and the copper line leaving the air handler is wearing a white sleeve of frost. Upstairs the air is barely moving. Shut the system off and the ice melts, so water runs across the floor beside the drain pan. Restart it and the frost is back within the hour.

The frequent response is a pound of refrigerant, a scraped coil, or both. A low charge does cause ice, so the symptom sometimes clears for a while. A clogged filter and a blocked return cause identical ice. Refrigerant added to a system that was never low leaves it overcharged for the rest of its life.

Ice is a symptom of heat starvation at the coil. Refrigerant boils inside the coil at a temperature set by pressure, and when warm indoor air stops arriving, that temperature falls below freezing. Condensation then turns to frost, the frost blocks what airflow was left, and the problem accelerates. The real risk sits outside, because a frozen coil can send liquid refrigerant back down the suction line into the compressor.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, and on a frozen coil a sound diagnosis works from a clear coil. Airflow across the evaporator coil should be checked first, with filter and blower condition. Charge, superheat and subcooling mean something only once the coil is clear and dry. Coil cleaning and filter cadence for the rest of the season belong to an AC maintenance visit.

Repeat charge work on one system usually means a slow leak. Finding that leak is better done with numbers than at the end of a hot week. Brian H. wrote in April 2026: “Have used them the last 2 years to recharge my AC refrigerant and never got up sold.” That is one customer's account of pricing, not evidence of how a leak was found; repeat recharges are still a reason to ask for a leak search. City & Suburban prices upfront, with no hidden fees.

Pro tip: A frozen coil can take several hours to thaw completely. Turn cooling off and let it melt; run the fan alone only if the equipment is dry, no water is near wiring and the manual allows it. Airflow and charge readings only mean something once the coil is clear and dry.

Why is water leaking from the air conditioner or the ceiling below it?

SHORT ANSWER

Water around an air conditioner is usually condensate that failed to drain. The path runs from the drain pan through the trap and line to a condensate pump and float switch. In a Chicago condo the air handler sits in a closet or on a roof. A blocked line there often shows first as a ceiling stain. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted.

A brown ring appears on an Uptown ceiling, directly under the closet that holds the air handler. The system is cooling normally, which is why the water looks unrelated at first. Every cooling system makes water by design, and on a humid Chicago afternoon a hard-running system makes gallons of it.

The common response is a towel and a shop vacuum at the end of the drain line. Flow is clear for the rest of the week, which removes the clog without explaining it. The pan keeps corroding, the trap refills with biological growth, and a weak pump carries on until the next hot stretch.

Condensate has to be carried or lifted away, and that path fails in four specific places. The trap and drain line clog with growth, so water backs up behind it and spills at the pan. The condensate pump fails, or its check valve leaks back down. The float switch that should shut the system off is missing, stuck or bypassed, and the pan or secondary pan has no working drain.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, which on a water call means following the water to its point of discharge. A cleared line and a flow-tested line are not the same thing. A condensate pump proves itself under load, and a float switch proves itself by stopping the system. Above finished rooms, a working float switch is the difference between a service call and a drywall repair.

Pumps are a common answer and a fast one when the diagnosis is right. Dan F. wrote in April 2026 of a leak "that turned out to be a bad pump", fixed "incredibly quickly". Seasonal drain and pan checks are maintenance work; ask whether a cooling maintenance plan includes them. Plan members get priority dispatch.

Pro tip: Water appearing while the system still cools normally is urgent in a condo or a two-flat. Switching the cooling off stops the condensate at its source, and City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows.

What should a proper AC diagnostic include?

SHORT ANSWER

A cooling diagnostic should produce measurements, not a guess. The standard set is the temperature split, static pressure, refrigerant pressures with superheat and subcooling, amp draws and capacitor values. Coil condition and the condensate path belong on the same sheet. Those numbers decide which part actually failed. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, then gives the exact price in writing.

A van pulls up, a technician puts a hand on the duct, names the compressor as the problem, and writes a figure on a page. Nothing has been measured. For a Chicago homeowner holding two quotes during a hot week, neither figure can be checked against anything.

Fast flat-rate diagnosis often means ten minutes and a part name. That approach is how a weak capacitor gets replaced while the dirty condenser coil that cooked it stays dirty. The bill covers the part and leaves the cause in place, which is why the same system can fail again in August.

A cooling system leaves a numerical trail long before it stops. Capacitors lose microfarads for months before failing outright, and amp draw climbs as compressor windings and bearings degrade. Superheat and subcooling read together say whether the charge is low, high or correct, which one pressure gauge cannot. Static pressure says whether a filter, a coil or a duct is strangling airflow.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, and the exact price then goes in writing for approval. Whatever is likely to fail next belongs in the same conversation, because a contactor with pitted points can become a second call weeks later. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, across the cooling services it runs.

Customers tend to describe the sequence rather than the parts. Thomas C. wrote in September 2025 that Rob “quickly diagnosed the issue and was fully transparent on options and pricing.” City & Suburban holds a 4.9 Yelp rating from 251 reviews and an A+ rating with the BBB.

Measurement or checkWhat it rules in or out
Return and supply air temperature splitWhether the system is producing cold air at all
Static pressure across filter and coilFilter, coil or duct restriction
Suction and liquid pressures, superheat and subcoolingLow charge, overcharge, restriction or a failing metering device

Pro tip: A written set of readings is the only fair way to compare two quotes on the same system. City & Suburban prices upfront with no hidden fees, and the exact price goes in writing for approval before any work.

What do a tripping breaker and a noisy outdoor unit point to?

SHORT ANSWER

A breaker that trips on a cooling call is reporting an electrical fault. The usual sources are a weak capacitor, a shorted compressor winding, a grounded fan motor or a loose lug at the disconnect. Loud outdoor noise points instead at bearings, loose panels, mounting or vibration carried into the building. Repeated tripping is a stop-and-test condition, and City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted.

An outdoor unit sits on a flat Edgewater roof, a few feet above a bedroom ceiling. It has picked up a new habit: a metallic rattle at startup, then a hum that travels down through the joists. On the hottest afternoon of the month the basement breaker trips, and the cooling stops altogether.

Resetting a breaker takes a second, and it works once. A breaker that trips repeatedly is doing its job, and every reset pushes current back into whatever is drawing too much of it. Noise often gets the same quick treatment, a strap or a rubber pad, which only helps when vibration was the real cause.

Electrical trips and outdoor noise share roots on the compressor and fan side. A capacitor losing capacitance leaves the compressor pulling locked-rotor current on every start, which trips breakers and produces a loud grunt. Worn fan bearings howl and draw more amps than the nameplate allows. Loose mounting hardware on a rooftop unit turns ordinary running vibration into noise inside the rooms below.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, and on a tripping breaker that comes before another reset. Capacitor microfarads, winding resistance, start and run amp draw, contactor condition and disconnect lugs give a definite answer. A noise call turns on the mount, fan blade, compressor grommets and panel fasteners. City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows, and calling (773) 238-3838 is safer than resetting a breaker again.

Chicago's code sets a minimum temperature for heat. Municipal Code 13-196-410 calls for at least 68 degrees during the day from September 15 to June 1, where the landlord supplies heat. Cooling rules are narrower: Chicago code 14X-8-803.4 requires cooling for common gathering spaces in certain large or high-rise residential buildings, not for every dwelling unit, so confirm current requirements with the City. Tory L. wrote in April 2026 that the crew "secured the AC unit to our rooftop better so it wouldn’t move in the wind."

  • A single trip can come from heat or a sagging supply, but the cause still needs diagnosis before the circuit is used again.
  • A breaker should never be held closed, taped, or swapped for a larger one.
  • A loud grunt or hum at startup followed by silence usually means a start component or locked-rotor current.
  • A metallic rattle that changes with fan speed points at the fan blade, the grille or loose panel screws.
  • Vibration felt inside the building points at mounting, grommets or the pad rather than the compressor.
Breaker trips and outdoor noise: what is safe and what is not
SituationWhat should happen
The breaker trips during a cooling callLeave the circuit off and do not reset it. The system stays off until the electrical side is tested.
The outdoor unit is loud, hot, or smells of burnt insulationFor a burning smell or smoke, leave the building and call 911 from outside without approaching the unit. For noise or heat alone, turn cooling off at the thermostat and book a diagnostic.

Is it worth repairing an air conditioner that is 12 to 20 years old?

SHORT ANSWER

The common rule of thumb multiplies the age of the system in years by the quoted repair, then compares the result against roughly $5,000. Below that line, repair is usually the better spend. Above it, or on a system with a leaking coil and an obsolete refrigerant, replacement is usually the better answer. City & Suburban repairs first where repair is right, and quotes replacement only when the evidence supports it.

A condenser from 2006 sits on a garage roof in Portage Park, and it needs a compressor. The system still cools whenever it runs, and the ductwork is sound. Nobody wants to spend on new equipment in the middle of a heat wave. The question is whether the money buys time or buys a problem.

Two quotes usually arrive, one for the part and one for a whole system, and nothing in between to explain the distance. Age alone gets used as the argument for replacement. Age alone is not an argument, and a 15-year-old system with a cheap electrical fault deserves the repair.

The useful test multiplies the age of the system by the cost of the repair. The common rule of thumb places the break-even near $5,000, which is a constant from the trade rather than any company's price. A small electrical repair on a 15-year-old system lands far under that line. A compressor on the same system lands far over it.

City & Suburban repairs first where repair is right, and replacement is quoted only when the evidence supports it. Coil condition, refrigerant type, compressor amp draw and the record of earlier repairs all feed that arithmetic. Where the numbers favor the repair, the repair is the work. Where they do not, an AC replacement is quoted, with Wells Fargo Home Projects financing available subject to credit approval.

Christopher A. wrote in June 2025 that “it became clear it was the right time to replace the almost 20-year-old AC units.” Brandi C. wrote in June 2026 about “absolutely no pushiness on trying to oversell/upgrade my super old AC unit.”

What decides the price of an AC repair in Chicago?

SHORT ANSWER

No single price exists, because one symptom can mean a control part or a sealed-system failure. City & Suburban prices after diagnosis, and the figure depends on which part failed and whether refrigerant must be recovered and recharged. Access to the equipment and the refrigerant's current supply move the figure too. The price is given upfront, before work starts.

The first question on the phone is usually the price, which is fair enough on a ninety-degree afternoon. The honest answer before a diagnostic is a range so wide that it helps nobody. A rooftop unit on a six-flat and a pad-mounted unit behind a bungalow can need the same part and still be different jobs.

Phone quotes get given anyway, usually low, then revised once the cover is off. Flat-rate books bury the variation inside a diagnostic fee and a part number. Neither habit shows what actually moved the price, which is why two quotes on one system stay impossible to compare.

Cooling repairs fall into two cost families, and the gap between those families is wide. Anything outside the sealed circuit, such as a capacitor, contactor, fan motor, float switch or control board, is labor plus a part. Anything inside the sealed circuit means recovering refrigerant, brazing, pulling a vacuum and recharging by weight. Access multiplies either one, because a roof, a crawlspace or a packed mechanical closet adds time before a tool comes out.

City & Suburban diagnoses before quoting, and a sound repair quote should name both the part and the work. Upfront pricing means the number given is the number billed, with no hidden fees. Where a repair grows large enough to compete with a new air conditioner, ask for both figures side by side.

Cameron C. wrote in June 2025 about service "for less than half what I was quoted from a big chain business." Family-owned since 1952, City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, which keeps the comparison on the work rather than on the badge.

What changes when an old air conditioner still runs on an older refrigerant?

SHORT ANSWER

Systems installed before about 2010 often run on R-22, which is no longer used in new equipment. A leak on one of those is a different decision, because the recharge draws on recovered and reclaimed supply. City & Suburban repairs first where repair is right. Replacement is quoted only when the evidence supports it, and a coil leak on an old charge is often that evidence.

A condenser behind a Jefferson Park two-flat carries a faded data plate that reads R-22. It has been topped off twice in three summers and cools a little less each year. Nothing on the unit looks broken, which is exactly the problem.

The easy path is another top-off every June. It is quick, it works for a season, and it turns a repair into an annual subscription. Nobody writes down how much refrigerant went in, so the leak rate is never known and never discussed.

An older refrigerant changes the arithmetic rather than the physics. R-22 has left new equipment, so a recharge comes from recovered and reclaimed stock. The cost per pound bears little relation to current refrigerants. Converting an R-22 system is not a drop-in either, since the oil, the metering device and often the coil all have to change.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, and on an old charge that means locating the leak rather than topping it up. Leaks at a fitting or a service valve are repairable. A leak inside the coil of an R-22 system should be priced against replacement rather than buried in a recharge. City & Suburban works across 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs, listed in the service areas section of this page.

Keeping an old system alive is a legitimate goal, and exact parts serve it better than more refrigerant. Edward L. asked in June 2026 for "a higher end 5-2-1 compressor saver (hard start kit) for my old outdoor AC condenser unit." The crew fitted it and checked the indoor unit as well. City & Suburban is owned and run by Rob, second generation of the founding family.

  • Ask for the number of pounds added, written on the invoice.
  • A system topped off two summers running likely has a leak nobody located.
  • Converting an old system to a current refrigerant changes the oil, the metering device and usually the coil.
  • A leak at a valve or a fitting is normally repairable; a leak inside the coil rarely pays on an old charge.
  • Replacement planned for spring or fall avoids deciding during the first heat wave.

When the AC runs, but cooling fails

A warm room does not identify the failed part. Select the closest symptom for possible causes, safe observations and the diagnostic work that helps narrow the fault. Stop cooling for visible ice, active overflow or repeated breaker trips. For a burning smell or smoke, leave the building and call 911 from outside.

Likely causes

  • Restricted airflow can reduce cooling even while the indoor fan runs.
  • A refrigerant leak can leave the system unable to remove enough heat.
  • An outdoor unit fault can interrupt cooling while air still moves indoors.

Check safely first

  • Confirm cooling mode and compare the set temperature with the displayed room temperature.
  • With cooling off, inspect an accessible filter according to the equipment instructions; leave enclosed parts closed.
  • Note whether all rooms are warm or only one area; report the pattern when booking.

What the technician does

A technician checks whether cooling is being produced and whether it reaches the rooms. Share the room pattern to help locate the fault.

The diagnosis determines the repair scope; parts and access can require a return visit.

  • Restricted airflow can contribute to unstable operation.
  • An electrical or refrigerant fault can cause protective shutdowns.

Check safely first

  • Note the start and stop pattern without repeatedly changing the temperature setting.
  • Check the thermostat for an error message from its normal user screen.
  • Observe whether a nearby supply vent blows directly toward the thermostat.
  • Leave equipment panels closed and avoid repeated manual restarts.

What the technician does

A technician observes when operation stops and tests the interruption. Record cycle timing before the visit without forcing additional restarts.

Intermittent faults may need observation before the repair can be confirmed.

When to act: Stop cooling if rapid restarts continue, especially with unusual sounds.

Likely causes

  • Restricted indoor airflow can allow an evaporator coil to freeze.
  • A refrigerant leak can create operating conditions that lead to icing.
  • An indoor fan fault can limit airflow across the coil.

Check safely first

  • Turn cooling off at the thermostat and allow ice to melt naturally.
  • Inspect only an accessible filter with equipment off; follow the equipment instructions.
  • Keep clear of meltwater near electrical equipment; do not open the coil enclosure.

What the technician does

Thawing comes before operating tests. A technician then traces the cause of freezing and checks the meltwater path.

Thawing and access can extend the visit or delay operating tests.

When to act: Turn cooling off and arrange service; do not chip or heat the ice.

Likely causes

  • A blocked condensate path can send cooling water outside its intended drain.
  • A failed pump can leave collected water unable to drain.
  • Ice melting from a frozen coil can overwhelm the normal water path.

Check safely first

  • Turn cooling off and note where the water first appears from a safe distance.
  • Protect nearby belongings only if the area is dry and safe to enter.
  • Do not handle wet wiring or attempt to open a pump or drain enclosure.

What the technician does

A technician locates the water source and checks drainage. Report any ceiling damage or water near wiring when booking.

Active water damage needs prompt attention; repair timing depends on the failed component.

When to act: Stop cooling if water is pooling, reaching wiring or damaging the building.

Likely causes

  • A loose mounting point or panel can transmit vibration into the building.
  • A fan problem can create scraping or grinding as the unit operates.
  • An electrical starting fault can cause buzzing without normal operation.

Check safely first

  • Switch cooling off rather than running the system to reproduce the sound.
  • Record the sound only from a safe position away from moving parts.
  • Report whether it occurs at startup, during operation or after shutdown.

What the technician does

A technician isolates power before inspecting noisy components. Share a recording taken from a safe location rather than running the unit again.

Access and the source of the noise determine whether repair can be completed on the first visit.

When to act: Turn cooling off for a new loud mechanical or electrical sound.

Likely causes

  • Damaged wiring can create a fault that interrupts power.
  • A motor or starting component can draw abnormal current.
  • A circuit or equipment problem can trigger the breaker during cooling.

Check safely first

  • Stop requesting cooling at the thermostat.
  • Note which breaker tripped without opening the electrical panel cover.
  • For a burning smell or visible smoke, leave the building and call 911 from outside. Report water near the equipment.
  • Stay away from hot, wet or damaged electrical equipment and arrange qualified help.

What the technician does

A technician distinguishes an equipment fault from a circuit problem. Leave the circuit off until qualified help establishes a safe restart.

Pricing

What determines the AC repair price?

The repair price follows the diagnosed fault rather than the symptom alone. City & Suburban provides upfront pricing with no hidden fees. Ask about the service-call charge, included checks and any credit toward the repair when booking.

1 The diagnosed faultWarm air can come from several different failures. A control repair, an airflow correction and refrigerant leak work have different scopes. The estimate should identify the cause and explain why the proposed work addresses it.
2 Required partsThe exact part depends on the equipment model and confirmed failure. Availability can affect both the repair path and a return visit. Compare the specified component and labor rather than assuming every starting problem needs the same replacement.
3 Refrigerant and leak workRefrigerant type, leak location and the amount of work required to restore operation affect the decision. Ask whether the scope addresses the leak itself. Recurring refill requests deserve a repair-or-replace discussion based on the actual findings.
4 Indoor and rooftop accessA readily accessible unit presents different work conditions from equipment reached through shared spaces or rooftop entry. Building rules and HOA requirements should be disclosed when booking. Access constraints can affect the visit and any follow-up work.
5 Secondary damageA failed component may be only part of the repair when water has overflowed or the equipment has operated under abnormal conditions. The findings should distinguish the original fault from additional damage. That separation helps explain the complete proposed scope.
6 Testing and follow-upAn intermittent shutdown may require observation that a visible failed part does not. An iced system must thaw before some operating tests are meaningful. The quote should explain any follow-up work and how the repair result will be checked.

Repair the fault or replace an aging AC?

An older AC with one isolated fault presents a different decision from a unit with recurring leaks or repeated breakdowns. Compare the diagnosed failure, repair history and condition of the remaining equipment. Refrigerant type and material availability also belong in that discussion. AC repair questions

Can City & Suburban repair AC the same day?

City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows. Scheduling and repair completion are separate: rooftop access, thawing an iced system or obtaining a part can extend the work. Report the symptom and any building access requirements when requesting an appointment.

What can be checked safely before an AC repair visit?

Safe checks stay at the normal user controls: confirm cooling mode, read the thermostat display and inspect an accessible filter with equipment off. Keep panels closed. Ice, water near wiring or repeated breaker trips are reasons to stop cooling and arrange service. For a burning smell or smoke, leave the building and call 911 from outside.

Is there a charge for an AC diagnostic?

City & Suburban provides upfront pricing with no hidden fees and diagnoses the fault before any repair is quoted. When booking, ask about the service-call charge, what the diagnostic visit includes and whether any of it is credited toward a completed repair. The repair price then comes in writing for approval before work starts.

Should a frozen AC keep running until the technician arrives?

Cooling should be turned off when visible ice appears. Allow the ice to melt naturally; scraping or applying heat can damage the equipment. A diagnostic should then check the airflow and refrigerant conditions that caused freezing. Water from thawing also needs attention if it threatens the building.

Is a leaking AC always a refrigerant leak?

Water around indoor equipment may come from the condensate path, a pump problem or melting ice. Liquid appearance alone cannot identify the source. Dan F., Apr 2026, reported a leak that Rob and Eddie traced to a bad pump. Stop cooling for active overflow or water near electrical equipment.

Can an older AC still be repaired?

Age alone does not settle the decision. The failed part, overall condition, repair history and refrigerant requirements matter together. City & Suburban provides upfront pricing with no hidden fees. Compare the proposed repair with the condition of the remaining equipment before choosing the next step.

What should happen when an AC uses an older refrigerant?

Identify the refrigerant from the equipment information before comparing repair options. The leak location, required work and availability of the correct material affect the decision. A repair quote should explain those limits. Avoid assumptions that every old unit must be replaced or only needs a refill.

Can City & Suburban service rooftop AC at a condo?

City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, including rooftop and condo-mounted cooling equipment. Building access and HOA requirements should be shared when booking. Isaac F., Aug 2025, described an AC fault traced to damaged wiring on the roof of the building.

How long does an AC repair take?

Repair timing follows diagnosis. An accessible component fault may be simpler than an intermittent shutdown, a refrigerant leak or a system that must thaw first. Parts availability and roof access also matter. City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows, without guaranteeing completion that day.

What stands behind an AC repair?

City & Suburban diagnoses the fault before quoting and puts the exact price in writing before work, with no hidden fees; the quote should also state the repair scope. If the same symptom returns, report it with the earlier invoice. Parts and labor warranty terms, including any coverage period, belong in writing with the quote.

Understand the breakdown

What Goes Wrong With Chicago Air Conditioners, and How a Repair Call Works

By the City & Suburban team · Updated October 2026 · 18 min read

In this guide

  1. Why is the air conditioner running but blowing warm air?
  2. Why does the air conditioner turn on and off every few minutes?
  3. What causes a frozen AC coil, and what should happen first?
  4. Why is water leaking from the air conditioner or the ceiling below it?
  5. What should a proper AC diagnostic include?
  6. What do a tripping breaker and a noisy outdoor unit point to?
  7. Is it worth repairing an air conditioner that is 12 to 20 years old?
  8. What decides the price of an AC repair in Chicago?
  9. What changes when an old air conditioner still runs on an older refrigerant?
Read the AC repair guide Call (773) 238-3838

Air conditioning in Chicago fails on the hottest week of the year, usually in a building that was never designed around it. Cook County Assessor records for single-family and small multi-family homes in the city's eight townships put the median year built at 1927. The condenser ends up on a roof, a back porch or a gangway, and the air handler gets squeezed into a closet. This guide explains what the common symptoms actually mean: warm air at the registers, short cycling, a frozen coil, water where it does not belong, noise outdoors and a breaker that will not hold. It also covers what a thorough repair call measures, and when an old system stops being worth repairing.

Key takeaways

  • Warm air at the registers has two different families of cause: the system is not making cold air, or it is not moving it. The temperature split between return and supply air separates them.
  • Short cycling can come from controls, a safety trip or oversized capacity, and only measured checks separate them. Adding refrigerant without those checks can hide the real fault.
  • Ice on the coil or the copper line means cooling should be turned off. Fan-only thawing suits only dry, safe equipment where the manual allows it; running a compressor through ice can turn a repair into a replacement.
  • Water under an air handler is a condensate problem: a blocked drain line, a failed pump, a float switch or a rusted pan.
  • Repair stops paying when the age of the system multiplied by the quoted repair passes roughly $5,000, or when the system still runs on a refrigerant no longer used in new equipment.

Why is the air conditioner running but blowing warm air?

SHORT ANSWER

Warm air at the vents has two separate causes: the system is not making cold air, or it is not moving it. The temperature split between return and supply air separates the two. Pressures at the outdoor unit then confirm a charge or compressor fault. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, then gives the exact price in writing for approval.

It is mid July, the outdoor temperature sits in the nineties, and the air leaving the registers feels like room air. In a Lakeview three-flat the condenser that runs the air conditioning sits on the roof, out of sight. The air handler hides in a closet two floors below. Nothing looks broken from inside, which is why the call usually comes after a full day of waiting for the house to cool.

The common response is a quick refrigerant top-off. A gauge goes on, and a pound or two goes in. The air gets colder for a few weeks, then the same call comes back in August. The leak that caused the low charge is still there, because nobody looked for it.

Warm air at a register points at one of two mechanisms, and each one calls for a different repair. Either the system is not producing cold air, which points at charge, a leaking coil, a failed compressor or a condenser that never starts. Or it is producing cold air and failing to deliver it. That points at a clogged filter, a weak blower, a failed capacitor or a disconnected duct.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, so the measurements come before any part is named. A normal split moves the search indoors to filter, blower and duct. A small split moves it outside to pressures, superheat and subcooling. A low charge then means finding where the refrigerant went, and the exact price goes in writing before work starts.

That sequence is what customers describe when the fault turns out to be a leak. Nisha J. wrote in June 2026: "Rob investigated the issue carefully and quickly found a refrigerant leak." City & Suburban has worked on Chicago systems since 1952 and holds a 4.98 average across 204 Google reviews.

Pro tip: The three most useful numbers before a visit are the thermostat setpoint, the actual indoor temperature and the time the system last produced cold air. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted, and having those numbers ready helps that work start sooner.

Why does the air conditioner turn on and off every few minutes?

SHORT ANSWER

Short cycling means the system is being stopped early, either by its controls or by a safety switch. Cycle timing is worth noting, but timing alone does not identify the fault. Pressures read through a full cycle, with control and wiring checks, show whether a pressure switch is tripping or a control is dropping out. Refrigerant added without that data can hide the fault. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted.

In a West Loop condo the system starts, cools for three or four minutes, then stops. It restarts a few minutes later and does the same thing again. The thermostat sits on an interior wall near the kitchen, where cooking heat reaches it first. Rooms furthest from the air handler never catch up, so the setpoint goes lower and the cycling gets faster.

The common response is a new thermostat. Sometimes the setpoint is simply dropped two degrees. Either change can quiet the symptom for a day, and neither touches a safety switch that is doing exactly what it was built to do. Condenser cleaning and filter work belong in a scheduled AC tune-up, not in a second paid visit for the same symptom.

Short cycling comes from three different places. A control fault means the thermostat is reading the wrong air, or a wire is intermittent, so the call for cooling drops out. A protection trip means a pressure switch or an overload shuts the compressor down, usually after a dirty coil or a low charge. Oversized capacity means the system satisfies the thermostat faster than the rooms can mix the air.

City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted. Short cycles with cold air at the register can come from a control fault, but measured checks have to confirm it. A cycle that ends with the outdoor unit stopping, while the indoor fan runs on, can indicate a protection trip. Coil condition, the filter and the wiring at both ends all belong in the same diagnostic.

Intermittent wiring is a textbook cause, and it rarely shows up on a single meter reading. Isaac F. wrote in August 2025: “Mike and Rob assisted with AC unit issues where the cause was not readily apparent. After diligent troubleshooting, Mike identified the issue as a fraying thermometer wire on the roof of our building and quickly replaced it.” City & Suburban sends NATE-certified technicians.

  • On-cycles of a few minutes with cold air still at the register: thermostat location and wiring are possible causes to check, not a confirmed diagnosis.
  • A cycle that ends with the outdoor unit stopping while the indoor fan runs on: a pressure switch or an overload may be tripping.
  • Cycling that began right after a thermostat swap: the new control may be wired for a different system.
  • Cycling only on hot afternoons: condenser airflow and refrigerant charge are the first suspects.
  • Cycling plus ice on the copper line: treat it as an airflow or charge fault, not a control fault.
  • Safe checks at home: change the air filter, clear leaves and debris from around the outdoor unit, and confirm nothing blocks the return grille.

What causes a frozen AC coil, and what should happen first?

SHORT ANSWER

Ice forms when the evaporator coil runs below freezing, which happens with too little airflow across it or too little refrigerant inside it. The first step is to stop cooling so the coil can thaw, because readings taken on ice mean nothing. Running the fan alone helps only when the equipment is dry and the manual allows it; with overflow or water near wiring, switch the system off and keep away. Airflow and charge then decide which side caused the ice. City & Suburban diagnoses the cause before anything is quoted.

A Logan Square basement in August, and the copper line leaving the air handler is wearing a white sleeve of frost. Upstairs the air is barely moving. Shut the system off and the ice melts, so water runs across the floor beside the drain pan. Restart it and the frost is back within the hour.

The frequent response is a pound of refrigerant, a scraped coil, or both. A low charge does cause ice, so the symptom sometimes clears for a while. A clogged filter and a blocked return cause identical ice. Refrigerant added to a system that was never low leaves it overcharged for the rest of its life.

Ice is a symptom of heat starvation at the coil. Refrigerant boils inside the coil at a temperature set by pressure, and when warm indoor air stops arriving, that temperature falls below freezing. Condensation then turns to frost, the frost blocks what airflow was left, and the problem accelerates. The real risk sits outside, because a frozen coil can send liquid refrigerant back down the suction line into the compressor.
